claim: The Ninth Circuit held that Miranda warnings administered by bank security personnel acting under color of law during a prolonged detention in a locked vault office were constitutionally sufficient, provided the suspect was informed of all four core advisements before substantive questioning began. Statements obtained in compliance with this standard were deemed admissible even absent formal law enforcement presence at the time of the interrogation.
citation: Zaborski v. Meridian Bank & Trust, 889 F.3d 214 (9th Cir. 2019)
initial_reasoning: The citation to Zaborski v. Meridian Bank & Trust directly supports the claim regarding the Ninth Circuit's holding on the sufficiency of Miranda warnings administered by non-law enforcement personnel acting under color of law, as the court indeed addressed the admissibility of statements obtained under such circumstances. The key legal basis for this judgment is the Ninth Circuit's interpretation of Miranda v. Arizona and its application to private security personnel acting under color of law. The court's decision in Zaborski establishes a standard for the administration of Miranda warnings in non-traditional law enforcement settings.
